Dec 2025 · Capstone · Retail

One report that takes leadership from company-wide revenue down to a single store manager or product group, with last year's number next to every figure.

Why I built it

KPIM Mart is a grocery and household-goods chain. Leadership needed one place to track revenue, orders, products sold and customers, and to see whether each region, store and manager was ahead of or behind last year.

What it helps with

A manager can pick a year and a KPI and immediately see which district, store or product group is driving the number, then hover any day on the trend to see that day's top 5 products. No separate reports per KPI.

Tools used

  • Power Querycleaned Excel exports, added columns
  • Snowflake schema2 fact tables: sales and sales plan
  • DAXField parameters, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, TOTALYTD

What the data shows 2022 view

  • 5.90bn VND revenue from 26.93K orders and 18.29K customers
  • Household goods bring in about 66% of revenue, far ahead of packaged food
  • Cầu Giấy district leads with 27% of revenue, followed by Hai Bà Trưng at 19%

How I built it

  • Field parameters switch every visual between Revenue, Orders, Products Sold and Customers, so there's one page instead of four
  • YoY growth table by manager and product group, built on SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and DIVIDE for safe division
  • Custom tooltip page shows daily revenue, growth and top 5 products when you hover the trend line
  • Slicers for region, store, category, promotion program and year

Jan 2026 · Capstone · Logistics

Shows the logistics team exactly where orders are stuck, by manager and by product category, in one live view.

Why I built it

Order tracking was split across 5+ manual reports. Nobody could quickly answer which orders were placed but not shipped, or delivered but not paid, and whose region they sat in.

What it helps with

The team sees bottlenecks by manager and category at a glance and can follow completion rate, order value and workload over time. Decisions that used to wait on a pile of reports now come from one screen.

Tools used

  • Power Query60,000+ rows transformed from Excel
  • DAX10+ status measures, e.g. Placed But Not Shipped
  • Bookmarks & slicers4 trend views; year, month, date range

What the data shows 2020 – 2022

  • 27,345 orders with a 99% completion rate overall
  • Food is 49% of orders and also holds the most open orders (1,058)
  • One regional manager carries 488 open orders, the heaviest load on the team

How I built it

  • Status measures for every stage: placed, delivered, paid, placed but not shipped, shipped but not delivered
  • Bookmarks toggle the trend chart between Order Value, Incomplete, Orders and Completion Rate without leaving the page
  • Side-by-side bars split open orders by manager and by category so the bottleneck has a name

The question behind it

"Completed" can hide problems. An order that was delivered but never paid still counts as delivered. So I split each stage into its own measure and put the two problem states (placed but not shipped, delivered but not paid) side by side for every manager.

That's what turns the dashboard from a scoreboard into a to-do list.

Dec 2025 · Capstone · Marketing

Groups KPIM Mart's customers by how recently, how often and how much they buy, so marketing knows who to keep, who to win back, and who to skip.

Why I built it

Marketing wanted to stop running the same promotion for everyone. KPIM Mart sells both everyday groceries and rare big-ticket appliances, so some customers buy often and cheap while others buy rarely and spend a lot.

What it helps with

Every customer gets a named segment and a one-line description, filterable by gender, card tier, income, occupation and education. Marketing can pull a target list for retention or win-back campaigns directly.

Tools used

  • Power BIstar schema, segment lookup table
  • DAXPERCENTILE.EXC scoring, RELATED lookup
  • Excelsegment definitions for 64 R-F-M combinations

The judgment call

Recency and Monetary are scored with percentiles. Frequency isn't. Most customers had only 1 or 2 orders, so percentiles would have crushed almost everyone into the bottom two scores and made the segments meaningless.

I used a plain business rule instead: 1 order scores 1, 4 or more scores 4. Combinations that don't map cleanly to a segment (like 2-2-3) stay as "Other" rather than being forced into a label.

-- Business rule, not percentiles
Score Frequency =
IF(dim_customer[Total Frequency] >= 4, 4,
  IF(dim_customer[Total Frequency] = 3, 3,
    IF(dim_customer[Total Frequency] = 2, 2,
      IF(dim_customer[Total Frequency] = 1, 1,
        BLANK()))))

What the data shows filtered view

  • Regular (30%), New high spending (27%) and New low spending (22%) are the biggest groups
  • Most valuable customers are only about 2%, which makes them cheap to protect
  • New high spenders are the clearest opportunity: one recent, large purchase and no repeat yet

How I built it

  • Four calculated columns in dim_customer: last purchase date, recency in days, order count, total spend
  • Recency scoring is inverted so the most recently active customers score 4
  • Segment table joins on the R-F-M key, so changing a segment rule never means rewriting DAX

2026 · Online learning platform

A single view of each teacher's activity on CompaClass: classes taught, blogs written, how many people read them, and how many students they bring in.

Why I built it

Program managers had no single place to see who was actually active. Teaching load, blog content and enrollment lived in separate places, so it was hard to tell who was carrying the platform.

What it helps with

Managers can compare teachers on content and teaching side by side, spot who writes a lot versus who teaches a lot, and trace each teacher's work back to real student sign-ups.

Tools used

  • Power BIKPI cards with year-over-year change
  • BookmarksClass / Course toggles on two visuals
  • Slicersyear, month, class, teacher

What the data shows 2025 view

  • Classes rose 61% (23 to 37) while active teachers fell 25% (8 to 6): fewer people carrying more load
  • Two teachers produce most blog views (2.2K and 2.1K)
  • The top class drew 201 enrollments, an advanced digital-skills course for a bank

How I built it

  • KPI cards show this year against last year with a colored arrow, so a drop is visible immediately
  • Scatter of blogs vs average views separates teachers who write often from teachers whose posts get read
  • Enrollment table links each class or course to its teacher and sign-up count
Nov 2025 · SQL only · Retail

Four Christmas seasons of gift sales (2018 – 2022) across 10 countries and 36 cities, analyzed entirely in SQL to plan the next holiday season.

Why I built it

Holiday sales are short and high-stakes. A retailer planning stock and promotions for the next Christmas needs to know which markets, channels and customer groups actually drove past seasons.

What it helps with

Gives holiday strategy and inventory planning a set of reusable queries: where to stock, which channel to push, and which day and hour to time campaigns for each age group.

Tools used

  • Azure SQL Databaseimported from Excel
  • Viewsseason flags, weekday, hour per transaction
  • CTEs, self-joins, window functionsgrowth and ranking
